# Prompting Ideogram

Models: Ideogram 4.0. A good prompt runs about 1500 characters.

Ideogram reads full sentences, and words near the start carry the most weight. It is the family to use when lettering matters. Sceneform turns Ideogram's own prompt expansion off, so the prompt reaches the model as written: supply the detail yourself.

**Order.** Open with one summary sentence that names the kind of image, the main subject and the tone, as if someone glanced at it for two seconds: "A product photo of a men's perfume bottle named "Nightlife for men" in a sleek studio setup." Then, in Ideogram's own order and dropping any part the request does not need: the subject's details (colour, shape, material, texture, and its text), its pose or action, the secondary props, the setting and background, the light and atmosphere, the framing and composition, and last the finish (lens effects, brush texture, line quality).

**Describe what can be seen.** Replace praise words with visible detail: "a red satin evening gown with intricate lace details", not "a beautiful dress"; "an impressionist painting with thick brushstrokes and pastel tones", not "a modern painting". Tie an abstract idea to an object or a pose: "a single flower blooming through a crack in the concrete" for hope. Ideogram draws what you name, so a precise word wins: "worm's-eye view", "cranberry red", "toddler" over "from below", "red", "young child".

**Text in the image.** Quote the exact words with the spelling and capitals they should have, and name them early: text near the start of the prompt comes out more reliably than text at the end. Say where it sits: "painted across the mural behind the artist", "curving along the bottom". Describe the lettering by weight, shape and mood ("bold sans-serif", "thin formal script with flourishes", "elongated 1960s hippie-style") rather than by a font name. Keep each string short, since every extra word raises the odds of a typo, and keep the scene around it simple. For several blocks, give each its own words, style and place, in reading order from the top down: "At the top, the headline "BLUE NOTE SESSIONS" in large gold serif capitals. Below the trumpeter, "Live jazz every Saturday night" in off-white italic serif. At the bottom, "THE VELVET ROOM" in small gold sans-serif capitals."

**Text limits.** Titles and short blocks render well; body copy and paragraphs do not. English is the most accurate. Keep non-Latin scripts and accented text to a word or two.

**Framing.** Everything you describe, Ideogram tries to show, even against the framing you asked for: mentioning boots turns a portrait into a full-length shot. Describe only what should be in frame, and name the framing outright ("head and shoulders", "full body", "wide view"). People who are small in the frame get distorted faces and hands, so move closer when they matter. For a poster, cover or other flat design, say the design fills the whole frame edge to edge: print words such as paper grain or ink registration can otherwise turn it into a photo of a printed poster on a wall.

**Emphasis.** When a key detail matters most, mention it in the summary and again in the details, and say where it sits.

**Settings stay out of the prompt.** Ideogram has no hidden syntax. Weights such as "::1", flags such as "--ar", and phrases like "16:9" or "four images" are read as ordinary words and change nothing.

**Avoid.** Negative phrasing: "a man without a beard" can give a beard, because the model latches onto the word after "no" or "without". Describe what you would see instead: "an empty room with chairs neatly arranged", "a robot with a smooth, featureless face". Contradictions such as "a clean, empty room cluttered with artifacts". Too many unrelated ideas in one prompt.
